name: Fat feminism
summary: Fat feminism holds that anti-fat prejudice is a feminist and political matter: stigma on fat bodies, especially women's, is produced by sexism and by the diet, fashion, insurance and medical industries, not by fat people's failings. It demands equal rights and an end to discrimination in work, education, public facilities and health care, treats dieting and weight-loss surgery as harmful and the reducing industries as the enemy, and claims power for fat people over their own bodies. It grew from 1970s radical feminism, the Fat Underground and radical therapy, and sees fat oppression as bound up with sexism, racism and class.
scope: The radical feminist fat liberation current: the Fat Underground (1973-83: Judy Freespirit, Aldebaran/Sara Fishman, Lynn Mabel-Lois, Gudrun Fonfa and others) and its manifesto and position papers, Karen Jones and Karen Stimson, 1980s feminist fat activists such as Kelly and Elana Dykewomon, and later writers in the fat liberation archive, as described by Charlotte Cooper's scholarship. Scoped to its own stated positions on weight stigma, discrimination, the diet and medical industries and bodily autonomy; it excludes NAAFA's reformist policy statements, Health at Every Size, commercial body positivity, and the wider left, whose positions are not borrowed.

sources.title: Fat Liberation Manifesto (1973)

sources.title: Job Discrimination (Fat Underground position paper, 1974)

sources.title: Sexism (Fat Underground position paper, 1974)

sources.title: Health of Fat Women...the Real Problem (Fat Underground position paper, 1974)
sources.author: Fat Underground
sources.usedFor: Accusation of medical and psychiatric malpractice; diet failure; fat as health-compatible.

sources.title: The Fat Underground Speaks (recording transcript)
sources.author: Fat Underground members

sources.title: Life In The Fat Underground (Radiance, 1998)

sources.usedFor: Founder's history: feminist perspective, alliance with the radical left, tactics against the diet industry, radical therapy.

sources.title: Fat Women and Feminism (Connecticut NOW Newsletter, 1974)
sources.author: Karen Jones
sources.usedFor: Argues fat is a feminist issue; sexist valuation of women, fear of fat used to divide women.

sources.title: They Are Trying to Kill Us (but it's for our own good) (Common Lives/Lesbian Lives, 1981)
sources.author: Kelly (Fat Liberator Publications)
sources.usedFor: Feminist fat liberation aims: decent health care, abolishing the diet industry; critique of Fat Is a Feminist Issue.

sources.title: Fat Feminism: Politics and Perspective (Largesse, archived)
sources.author: Karen Stimson
sources.usedFor: Fat feminist account: size discrimination is sexist, racist and classist; mainstream feminism's embrace of thinness.

sources.title: Fat, Fitness and Exercise: health or healthism? (Ample Apple, 1983)
sources.author: Karen Scott-Jones (Stimson)
sources.usedFor: Right to decide whether and how to exercise and eat; rejection of healthism.

sources.title: What's Fat Activism? (University of Limerick Sociology Working Paper WP2008-02)
sources.author: Charlotte Cooper
sources.usedFor: Scholarly history of fat liberation: radical feminist origins, bio-medical model, stakeholders, lobbying, intersectionality, anti-discrimination law.

sources.title: Book Review: Fat Activism: A Radical Social Movement by Charlotte Cooper (LSE Review of Books)
sources.author: Dimitrinka Atanasova
sources.usedFor: Scholarly account of the movement's radical feminist origins and divisions over healthism.

sources.title: Elana Dykewomon, Fat Liberation People's History interview (2022)
sources.author: Elana Dykewomon, interviewed by Tracy Tidgwell and Max Airborne
sources.usedFor: Fat oppression as one of the interlinking oppressions; fat treated as a side issue by other radical movements.

sources.title: Fat People Must Become a Priority to the Left (2019)
sources.author: Da'Shaun Harrison
sources.usedFor: Fat liberation writer's argument that anti-fatness must be a priority for left and feminist movements.

sources.title: Fat Underground Throws Weight Into Obesity War (Los Angeles Times, 1976)
sources.author: Jane Wilson
sources.usedFor: Contemporary report: members radical feminists, aims against medical and diet establishment.

sources.title: Fat Liberation Manifesto (1973)
sources.author: Judy Freespirit and Aldebaran / Fat Underground
sources.usedFor: Equal dignity, discrimination, industry accountability and bodily control; solidarity is not a general economic or foreign-policy programme.

sources.title: Life in the Fat Underground (1998)
sources.author: Sara Golda Bracha Fishman
sources.usedFor: Founders own account of sexist institutions, medical authority, collective organising and rejection of dieting as a solution to oppression.

sources.title: A Fat Womens Problem-Solving Group: Radical Change (1978)
sources.author: Aldebaran, Gudrun Fonfa and Reanne, with Simone Wallace, Merry Demarest and Syd Jasso
sources.usedFor: Fat feminist political analysis and liberated eating; not medical advice or proof of the texts empirical claims.

sources.title: Fat Feminist Herstory (1993)
sources.author: Karen W. Stimson / Largesse
sources.usedFor: Movement participants history, including feminist caucus abortion-rights organising and lesbian/bisexual fat liberation.

sources.title: Fat
sources.author: Charlotte Cooper
sources.usedFor: A defining contemporary activist-scholar describes intersectional fat feminism and distinguishes it from psychoanalytic pathologisation.

sources.title: A conversation about fat activism among activists in community with Nolose (2021)
sources.author: Sarah Doherty, Shana McDavis-Conway, Adrienne Hill, Elaine Lee, Sydney Lewis, Aaminah Shakur and Cicely Smith; Fat Studies 10(3):328–347
sources.usedFor: Contemporary queer fat feminist activists explain interlocking oppressions and material barriers to access; their individual unrelated affiliations do not answer for the whole movement.

sources.title: Campaign for Size Freedom
sources.author: NAAFA and FLARE
sources.usedFor: Present-day demands for enforceable size-discrimination protections; broader NAAFA positions are not automatically fat feminist positions.

missingStatements.text: Body size or weight should be a legally protected ground against discrimination in employment, education, public facilities and health services.
missingStatements.rationale: The manifesto demands equal rights and an end to discrimination against fat people in those four areas, and Cooper records activists campaigning for weight antidiscrimination legislation.

missingStatements.text: Weight-loss companies and professionals should be required to publish long-term evidence that their products work.
missingStatements.rationale: The manifesto demands that the reducing industries take responsibility for false claims and publish long-term studies proving any statistical efficacy.

missingStatements.text: Doctors should not treat weight loss as the default answer to a patient's health problems.
missingStatements.rationale: The Fat Underground's papers and later fat feminist accounts accuse doctors of answering every complaint with a diet instead of treating the condition.

missingStatements.text: A person's body size is determined mainly by biology rather than by eating habits or willpower.
missingStatements.rationale: The Fat Underground held that fat people eat no more than thin people on average and that fatness is largely inherited and permanent.

notes:
Searched: manifesto and Fat Underground position papers (sexism, jobs, health, psychiatry), interviews and recordings, 1970s-80s feminist fat activist essays, Cooper's scholarship and a review of her book. The sources are almost wholly about weight stigma, discrimination, the diet and medical industries, sexism and bodily autonomy; they record no position on elections, courts, federalism, war, alliances, aid, trade, welfare, taxes, unions, ecology or technology, so those are null. The old audit's economic answers (minimum wage, unions, taxes) were deductions from solidarity with the left and are dropped. Strands differ on healthism (Scott-Jones, Cooper) and on NAAFA's reformism against the Fat Underground's radicalism; fat feminists are also divided on whether fat is a disability and whether commercial body positivity helps.
